slides.title: A request has a creation time and a running time
keyPoints: Move the marker only when the queue is played
Retain enough information to reverse a successful move
Keep every position within 0 through 10
slides.narration: Imagine a planning screen with a marker at zero. A student selects move to three, then move to seven, but playback has not started. The screen should still show zero. This is the first distinction: asking for work and doing work may happen at different times. We also want undo, which brings a second requirement. After both requests run, undoing only the latest one must show three, not zero. A request must therefore retain its destination before execution and learn the previous position during execution. Today we will follow those two kinds of data separately, because mixing their timing creates a believable but wrong history.
actions: Ask learners to name the two moments before introducing a Command object.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch14.json → The problem: moving a marker is easy until timing changes

question.prompt: What must the marker show after two requests are created but neither is executed?
question.answer: Zero. Construction records intent; execution performs the change.

slides.title: Start with direct calls
keyPoints: A checked setter is enough for immediate work
Validation belongs to the marker rule
No history exists merely because values changed
slides.narration: This small program deliberately has no command class. The setter takes a reference, so assigning position changes the integer in main rather than a private copy. Its target parameter is a value: an independent integer argument. The range check runs before assignment, keeping the marker valid even if the caller supplies eleven. The two calls immediately change zero to three and then seven. That meets the immediate-work requirement, and a larger architecture would add no value yet. Notice what is absent: the program has neither a stored request nor the earlier positions. Knowing that the final position is seven does not tell us where it was before.
actions: Predict both output lines, then Run.

question.prompt: Can the final value seven tell us whether the previous position was three or five?
question.answer: No. Both histories can end at seven, so reversal needs retained information.

slides.title: A queue of integers is still a valid alternative
keyPoints: Destinations alone can describe move-only work
A rename needs different arguments and behavior
Store each request with the work it knows how to do
slides.narration: Suppose the only new requirement is delayed movement. A vector of destination integers and a loop over the checked setter is enough. We should keep that option on the table. The pressure for Command appears when one queue must also rename a marker or change its color, or when each request has its own reversal rule. Now a plain integer does not describe every request. Separate action-code and argument arrays can drift apart. A command object groups one request's data with its execute operation. The shared interface lets the playback loop trigger different requests without knowing each concrete type. The benefit is a stable place for execution policy, not an automatic guarantee of undo.
actions: Compare one move-only queue with a mixed move-and-rename queue.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch14.json → The problem: moving a marker is easy until timing changes

question.prompt: Does needing a queue alone force the use of inheritance?
question.answer: No. A move-only vector or a callable queue can be enough. A common command interface is useful when varied requests need a shared contract.

slides.title: The wrong saved value can look reasonable
keyPoints: Both requests are created while the position is zero
Saving prior state during construction is too early
Undoing the second request must restore three
slides.narration: The demo models the timing bug without unsafe memory access. It saves before_first and before_second while constructing the planned work, so both integers become zero. Only afterward do the moves run. The second request really follows position three, but its stored record cannot know that yet. The printed wrong undo result is zero; the correct isolated undo of the second move would be three. Moving the capture into execute fixes the timing. Do not fix this by changing the expected answer to zero. The required history is about successful execution order, and that order can differ from object construction order in a real event queue.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Keep marker positions within 0 through 10.
Construction must not execute a request.
Undo applied moves in reverse order and reject invalid command states.
slides.narration:
An undoable queue of marker moves. Move holds the receiver, destination, prior position, and an applied flag. The queue owns commands but borrows no internal marker storage. Receiver validation happens before the command commits success.

Keep marker positions within 0 through 10. Construction must not execute a request. Undo applied moves in reverse order and reject invalid command states.

The marker stays within its allowed range. Only successful executions set applied_ true. Commands must not outlive their borrowed receiver. Undo history assumes no unrelated edits to the receiver. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. A vector of integers with a loop is sufficient for a fixed set of move-only requests. A std::function<void()> queue is compact for delayed work, but an undo contract still needs saved state and pairing between forward and reverse behavior.

comparisons.text: Move holds the receiver, destination, prior position, and an applied flag. The queue owns commands but borrows no internal marker storage. Receiver validation happens before the command commits success.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Command implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: The marker stays within its allowed range. Only successful executions set applied_ true. Commands must not outlive their borrowed receiver. Undo history assumes no unrelated edits to the receiver.

slides.title: The problem: moving a marker is easy until timing changes
keyPoints: A planning screen shows a marker at an integer position from zero through ten.
A vector of destination integers can delay this one operation.
slides.narration:
A planning screen shows a marker at an integer position from zero through ten. Moving it immediately is simple: call marker.set(7). The setter rejects values outside the range and otherwise stores the new position. That direct call is the right first design when every request happens now and never needs undo. The new requirements are different: collect several moves, perform them later in order, and let the user undo that group in reverse order. The program must also reject a second execution of a move that is already applied.

A vector of destination integers can delay this one operation. However, if the screen later queues a rename or a color change, a vector of integers no longer describes all actions. A growing collection of parallel arrays for action codes and arguments is easy to misalign. The missing idea is to store a request together with the data and behavior needed to carry it out. That stored request is a command. We introduce an interface only because a single queue may need different kinds of requests with the same execute and undo operations.

question.prompt: Why should adding a move to a queue not immediately move the marker?
question.answer: The requirement separates scheduling from execution. A queued request records what should happen later; the receiver changes only when the queue executes that request.

slides.title: A command has intent before it has a history
keyPoints: Move stores a borrowed Marker reference and a target position.
The interface has virtual execute and undo functions, so callers can use a Command reference without knowing which concrete request it holds.
slides.narration:
Move stores a borrowed Marker reference and a target position. Its constructor records intent but does not move the marker. The reference means there is one actual marker: copying the marker into each command would create private markers and leave the screen unchanged. target_ is stored by value so a later change to a caller variable cannot silently change the queued destination. before_ becomes meaningful only when execute runs. Saving it during construction would record the wrong old position for the second command in a delayed queue.

The interface has virtual execute and undo functions, so callers can use a Command reference without knowing which concrete request it holds. A virtual destructor allows deletion through the base type. Move uses override to ask the compiler to confirm that its functions truly replace those interface functions. std::unique_ptr<Command> owns each queued command. The vector owns its smart pointers, while each command merely borrows the marker. In main the marker is declared before the queue and is destroyed after it, so all borrowed references remain valid.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch14.json → Execution has a commit point
slides.title: Execution has a commit point
keyPoints: Move begins with applied_ false.
This order is not cosmetic.
slides.narration:
Move begins with applied_ false. execute first rejects a repeated call. It then saves the current marker position, asks the marker to accept the target, and only after success sets applied_ true. This last step is a commit point: the flag now says there is a completed change that can be undone. If the setter rejects eleven, the marker remains unchanged and applied_ remains false. before_ may have been refreshed, but it does not authorize undo because the flag is still false.

This order is not cosmetic. Setting applied_ true before the setter succeeds would mark a failed request as part of the undo history. Updating the marker before validating the target would allow an invalid state even if an exception is thrown afterward. Here the setter validates first and then assigns one integer, which cannot throw. The program therefore gives a clear guarantee for a bad target: the visible marker stays as it was. This guarantee depends on the receiver behavior; a command cannot make a partly failing external service atomic merely by adding a bool.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch14.json → Undo reverses successful requests in reverse order
slides.title: Undo reverses successful requests in reverse order
keyPoints: The first queued move records zero and sets three.
An undo operation is permitted only for an applied command.
slides.narration:
The first queued move records zero and sets three. The second records three and sets seven. To reverse the group, undo the second move to restore three, then undo the first to restore zero. The reverse iterators rbegin and rend traverse the vector from its last element toward its first. In (*it)->undo(), *it obtains the unique pointer stored at the iterator position; the arrow accesses the owned command. Iteration changes which command is selected, not who owns it.

An undo operation is permitted only for an applied command. After restoration, applied_ becomes false and another execute is allowed; that is the limited redo behavior of this implementation. Redo reads a new before_ value at execution time. It does not promise to replay the exact historical environment. The design assumes exclusive, ordered changes to this marker while a history is active. If unrelated code changes the marker to nine between execution and undo, blindly restoring before_ can erase that later change. Real editors often route all edits through one history owner or use version checks to detect conflicts.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch14.json → Queueing, undo, and transactions are separate promises
slides.title: Queueing, undo, and transactions are separate promises
keyPoints: The primary queue loop runs commands in order but does not automatically undo earlier commands if a later one fails.
A command can also represent an operation that cannot truly be undone.
slides.narration:
The primary queue loop runs commands in order but does not automatically undo earlier commands if a later one fails. A transaction is a group treated as one success or failure under a stated contract. The lab adds a small transaction runner for range failures: it counts successfully applied commands and reverses only that prefix. An empty batch succeeds without changing the marker. A batch containing targets six and eleven returns failure and restores the original zero. This works because the local receiver and undo operations have tightly controlled behavior.

A command can also represent an operation that cannot truly be undone. Sending a message may be followed by a correction, but the recipient may already have read it. A compensation is a new action that tries to offset an earlier effect; it is not time travel. Another option for local state is a snapshot, developed in Chapter 17, which remembers the state instead of how to reverse each action. For this marker, two integers and a flag are cheaper and clearer than a general snapshot system. Choose what must be preserved before promising undo to a user.

question.prompt: What additional test is needed for a batch starting from position one?
question.answer: Fail after two successful moves and assert rollback reaches one, not zero. This catches implementations that reset to a hard-coded default instead of restoring history.

slides.title: One owner of commands; one borrowed receiver
keyPoints: The vector owns unique_ptr command handles
Each Move borrows the same Marker
The Marker must outlive every command that can run
slides.narration: In the chapter program, the queue owns its command objects through unique_ptr. Ownership means responsibility for ending those objects' lifetimes. A Move holds Marker&, which is a reference to the real marker, not ownership of it and not a copy. This is why two commands affect one visible position. The marker is declared before the queue in main. Local objects are destroyed in reverse declaration order, so the commands disappear before their receiver. If an application returned this queue while destroying a local marker, no smart pointer around the commands would save the borrowed reference. Review the lifetime of the receiver separately from the lifetime of the requests.
actions: Trace destruction order from main back to the Marker declaration.

question.prompt: Does unique_ptr<Command> keep the referenced Marker alive?
question.answer: No. It owns only the command object. The marker needs a separate lifetime guarantee.

slides.title: Dispatch is checked twice in different ways
keyPoints: virtual declares runtime selection through the interface
override checks the replacement signature at build time
A virtual destructor supports owned base pointers
slides.narration: The queue sees Command, while the object behind each pointer is a Move. Calling execute through that interface selects Move::execute during execution; this selection is virtual dispatch. Earlier, during compilation, override asks the compiler to check that the function really replaces a matching virtual function in the base class. These are different jobs. The compiler cannot prove that saving before_ at the wrong time preserves history. The virtual destructor matters when unique_ptr<Command> deletes a concrete command through the base type. The interface is therefore more than a name shared by methods: it defines both callable behavior and safe destruction through the chosen owning handle.
actions: Have learners classify signature errors and incorrect history as build-time or runtime evidence.

question.prompt: Would override detect setting applied_ before the receiver accepts the target?
question.answer: No. override checks a function relationship, not the behavioral order inside the function.

slides.title: Commit after the receiver succeeds
keyPoints: Check repeated execution first
Read prior state, then call the checked setter
Set applied_ only after normal return
slides.narration: Treat applied_ as a claim backed by evidence. False means this command currently has no completed change to reverse. execute checks that claim, reads the current position, and asks Marker to apply the destination. Only a successful return permits the assignment applied_ equals true. With destination eleven, Marker throws before assignment; the command remains unapplied and undo must reject it. This ordering provides a useful guarantee because the receiver validates before changing one integer. If a receiver instead wrote half a file before throwing, this flag would not repair the file. The command's guarantee can be no stronger than the receiver and recovery behavior it actually controls.
actions: Trace the exception path and cross out every statement it skips.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch14.json → Execution has a commit point

question.prompt: After execute rejects eleven, may undo restore before_?
question.answer: No. The command never committed success; undo must reject the unapplied state.

slides.title: Reverse the effects, not the display order
keyPoints: Successful changes form an ordered history
Newest successful change must be reversed first
Unrelated edits can invalidate saved history
slides.narration: After moves to three and seven, the first command remembers zero and the second remembers three. Reverse traversal first asks the second command to restore three, then the first to restore zero. In the source, rbegin starts at the newest queue entry and rend marks the reverse end. The expression (*it)->undo first obtains the smart pointer at the iterator position, then calls through it. If undo runs in forward order, the first restoration gives zero and the second overwrites it with three. Even correct reverse order assumes nobody independently changed the marker. A background edit to nine can be lost unless the application routes edits through one history or checks a version.
actions: Write the saved values beside the two commands and undo in both orders.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch14.json → Undo reverses successful requests in reverse order

question.prompt: Why is the final value three evidence of forward-order undo?
question.answer: The first command restores zero, then the second command overwrites it with its saved value three.

slides.title: A batch needs a stronger contract than a loop
keyPoints: A queue can stop after partially applied work
Count successful commands after execute returns
Rollback only the successful prefix, in reverse
slides.narration: The primary queue loop does not promise all-or-nothing behavior. In the extension, a transaction-like batch applies fresh commands in order and remembers how many completed. The counter increases only after execute returns. For targets six and eleven, one command succeeds and one throws, so rollback undoes exactly the first. It never attempts to undo the failing command. The lab catches the stated range error, not every possible error in the universe. This small contract works because the receiver's saved positions remain valid and undo does not fail under the stated assumptions. A production batch needs an explicit response to rollback failure; catching an exception does not erase that design question.
actions: Ask why incrementing the count before execute would break rollback.

question.prompt: For targets [6,11] from zero, how many commands are reversed?
question.answer: One: the successful move to six. The failed move to eleven is unapplied.

slides.title: Map the roles to the actual types
keyPoints: Command interface → Command::execute and undo
Concrete command → Move
Receiver → Marker
Invoker → main execution and reverse-undo loops
Client → main command construction
slides.narration:
Command interface → Command::execute and undo. Give the invoker a common operation. The chapter adds undo explicitly; it is not supplied automatically by virtual dispatch.

Concrete command → Move. Retain request data. Move also remembers the previous position and whether its request was successfully applied.

Receiver → Marker. Perform and validate domain changes. The marker enforces position bounds independently of how a request was triggered.

Invoker → main execution and reverse-undo loops. Decide when commands run. The queue owns stored commands; the loops supply the invoker behavior without a separate class.

Client → main command construction. Bind concrete requests to a receiver, then hand them to code working through the Command interface.

Representing requests explicitly gives a debugger a concrete place to inspect their arguments and state. Keep the history owner responsible for ordering and receiver lifetime instead of scattering undo calls across user-interface components.

question.prompt: Explain Command without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Move holds the receiver, destination, prior position, and an applied flag. The queue owns commands but borrows no internal marker storage. Receiver validation happens before the command commits success. A vector of integers with a loop is sufficient for a fixed set of move-only requests. A std::function<void()> queue is compact for delayed work, but an undo contract still needs saved state and pairing between forward and reverse behavior.

slides.title: Choose the smallest history that satisfies the promise
keyPoints: Immediate fixed action: direct call
Delayed action: stored request or callable
Undo: saved state or a valid inverse
slides.narration: Command is useful when the request itself must travel: through a queue, a menu action, a macro, or a controlled history. It is not a requirement for every setter call. A callable can represent delayed work compactly, but pairing it with reversal still needs a contract and retained information. An absolute move to seven cannot be undone by subtracting seven unless the previous position happened to be zero. Saving the old position expresses the real operation. For larger state, Chapter 17's snapshots may be clearer. For a remote message, a later correction is compensation, not true reversal. Choose among these designs by what the user has been promised, not by the pattern name.
actions: Ask for one requirement that would justify replacing that vector.

question.prompt: When is a vector of integers better than a command class hierarchy?
question.answer: When all queued requests are the same simple move operation and no per-type execution or undo behavior is needed.

slides.title: Debug the claim, the timing, and the owner
keyPoints: Wrong intermediate undo: inspect capture timing
False undo history: inspect the commit point
Crash after delayed execution: inspect receiver lifetime
slides.narration: A useful debugging session separates three failures. If undoing the second move jumps straight to zero, inspect when before_ was captured. If an invalid request can be undone, inspect when applied_ became true. If delayed execution touches a dead object, inspect who owns the receiver and how long the queue can survive. These failures require different repairs, even though they appear near the same command class. Add a focused test for each path: construction leaves the marker unchanged, a failed execute cannot be undone, and the execution owner never retains requests past receiver lifetime. Do not rely only on the final group-undo value; the early-capture bug can accidentally restore zero after both wrong undos.
actions: Require an intermediate assertion at position three.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch14.json → Execution has a commit point

question.prompt: Why is checking only the final zero after undoing both moves too weak?
question.answer: Both wrongly captured records may be zero. The final result passes while the intermediate undo of the second command is wrong.

slides.title: Explain Command without naming its classes
keyPoints: A stored request binds arguments to behavior
Execution establishes the history that undo consumes
The invoker controls when; the receiver enforces valid state
slides.narration: Close the code and describe the design in ordinary words. We keep a request so someone else can decide when it runs. The request holds its destination and a way to reach the real object. When it runs, it records the prior state, asks for a valid change, and marks success only afterward. Undo reverses successful changes under a stated ordering and isolation rule. That explanation is stronger than reciting client, invoker, and receiver. Now transfer it to a drawing editor: a menu and a keyboard shortcut can create the same action, while one history controls its timing. The editor still needs its own rules for document lifetime and edits arriving outside that history.
actions: Give learners one minute to explain the pattern without using its name.

question.prompt: What must you explain before promising undo for a new command?
question.answer: The retained information, successful commit point, receiver lifetime, ordering and isolation rules, and whether the external effect can actually be reversed.

graph.title: A queue owns requests; requests borrow the marker
graph.caption: The ownership edge ends at Command because that is the queue element type. Actual owned objects are Move instances. The inheritance arrow points from Move toward its base. The dependency arrow is a borrowed reference: deleting a command must never delete the marker. The invoker role belongs to the execution loops over queue, not to std::vector itself; main also performs the separate client role when constructing commands.
